transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-31 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~60 minutes
Attendees: Ethan Cole (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Jamal Rivers (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (CTO - Streamline), Liam O'Neill (Lead ML Eng), Sofia Ruiz (DevOps), Noah Park (PM)

[00:00] Ethan: hey everyone, thanks for jumping on, i'm ethan from redwood, i'll keep this short — priya and jamal will do the deep bits.
[00:05] Maya: thanks, yeah we've read the deck, excited to see the edgecases flow, especially long context and streaming under load.
[00:12] Priya: cool; agenda is long-context behavior (kv cache, memory), high TPS throughput (dedicated vs hosted), streaming backpressure & client-side timeouts, and then q&a. sound good?
[00:20] Liam: yep, we have a few constraints: we need predictable 99th perc latencies under 200ms for inference and we want to test 1k-5k TPS sustained, plus some 10k bursts. context windows are often 32k tokens or higher for a subset of use cases.
[00:33] Priya: got it. quick callout — we treat long-context in two ways: runtime optimizations (kv cache, prefix caching) and model variants (segmented context or sliding-window fallback). we'll show what that looks like in the console and through the api.
[00:45] Jamal: i'll start a quick demo of the console: here's a live trace view, per-route token breakdown, and the prefix cache hit rate panel — you can see how repeated prefixes avoid re-computation.
[01:00] Jamal: oh, quick note, the console autoplot labels sometimes show 'KV chache' in older logs — minor transcription quirk, but the metric is the prefix cache hit.
[01:10] Maya: nice, can we see how batching impacts tail latency? we can't sacrifice p99 for bulk throughput.
[01:18] Priya: yes — we have continuous batching with adaptive thresholds; for latency-sensitive routes we lower batch windows, for throughput we increase. in the demo i'll show a policy that routes by latency SLO.
[01:30] [Screen share pause to configure demo]
[02:10] Priya: ok i'm kicking off a synthetic benchmark — workload sim with a mix of long-context (32k) and short prompts, target 2k TPS. watch the error and retry panel.
[02:35] Liam: question — what happens when the streaming client can't keep up? our consumers sometimes are slow, so backpressure is common.
[02:45] Jamal: good question. we implement backpressure strategies at multiple layers: runtime-level shedding (reject), buffering with bounded queues, and graceful degradation to smaller model variants. the streaming SDK has a configurable client buffer and a reconnect/retry policy.
[03:05] Sofia: and client timeouts? if client disconnects mid-stream, do we continue compute?
[03:12] Priya: by default we stop compute to save units when the client disconnects, but there's an option to keep finalizing the token stream for audit logs or consistency — that costs tokens. default = abort-on-disconnect.
[03:28] Maya: for our use case we need both: if the user disconnects we want a persisted summary for later, but don't want to pay for huge re-compute often. any built-in dedupe?
[03:40] Jamal: we have a prefix/KV cache to reuse shared context; also request fingerprinting and idempotency keys to avoid double-charging on retries.
[03:50] Noah: what about timeouts on the platform side — connection timeouts vs model timeouts?
[03:56] Priya: we expose route-level timeout settings in the console and API. there is a hard compute timeout per model instance to protect against runaway generation and an overall request timeout that can trigger fallback models. you can set these in milliseconds per route.
[04:12] Maya: show us a real failure scenario — streaming backpressure + timeout.
[04:18] [Priya triggers a stress test: 3k TPS with many 32k prompts, emulated slow clients]
[05:00] Priya: ok you can see in the trace a spike — buffering queues hit threshold, we start shedding best-effort requests and route critical routes to Dedicated pool. note the model fallback rule — when latency >250ms we switch to a lower-quant (faster) variant.
[05:28] Liam: how does quantization affect hallucinations / quality for us? we have non-negotiable accuracy for some prompts.
[05:36] Jamal: tradeoff — INT8/FP16 quant reduces cost and improves throughput; we recommend hybrid policies: quantize non-critical routes, and keep full precision for high-sensitivity routes. Optimize will suggest profiles based on evals.
[05:52] Maya: are these suggestions automatic? can we trust Optimize to not regress?
[05:57] Priya: Optimize runs evals on historical prompt sets and surfaces expected token/sec improvements with quality deltas; you can veto, and we support A/B rollouts with canary traffic. we also tie regression alerts to evaluation suites so you'll get notified if quality drops beyond thresholds.
[06:15] Noah: what's the Dedicated capacity scenario? we'd prefer predictable throughput for our critical routes.
[06:22] Ethan: Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools with burst capacity; SLA-backed latency and throughput. for the 1k-5k TPS you described, we'd size based on tokens/sec distribution — we can propose a monthly reserved profile + burst credit for spikes.
[06:38] Sofia: and network isolation? we need VPC peering and KMS.
[06:43] Ethan: yes — Private deployments or Dedicated in a VPC with customer-managed KMS, SAML SSO, and audit logs are supported. we have SOC2 docs, and i'll attach the whitepaper after.
[06:55] Liam: ok, let's talk error modes: timeouts mid-stream cause partial outputs, how do we reconcile results for downstream systems?
[07:02] Priya: typical pattern: stream tokens with sequence numbers; on reconnect you can request missing ranges or use the cached partial result. we also send event hooks to your webhook for partial completions.
[07:20] Maya: any limits on context >32k? we sometimes need 64k for doc retrieval.
[07:27] Jamal: some model families that we curate can handle 64k with more memory and different kernel selection; runtime will select model variant and kernel to fit the sequence distribution. cost goes up linearly-ish and you should expect throughput to drop. we can recommend chunking strategies or sparse attention variants.
[07:48] Liam: can you show logs for a case where we hit compute timeouts?
[07:55] [screen shows logs with a 'timeout' event and fallback kick-in]
[08:20] Priya: you can see the timeline: request arrives, queued, started computing, then at 12s we hit compute timeout so fallback model returned a shorter response and a flag shows 'degraded_response'.
[08:35] Maya: that's helpful. do we get metrics per-token cost and p99 by route?
[08:40] Jamal: yes, cost by token, per-route p50/p95/p99, and a token-level breakdown (context vs generated).
[08:48] Noah: curious about streaming backpressure to the client — are we talking TCP level or application-level?
[08:53] Priya: both; the streaming SDK uses application-level flow control over websockets or http/2 streaming. if your client is slow at consuming frames, the server's buffer will fill and then the runtime enforces backpressure policies. you can configure drop, buffer, or block-with-timeout. we typically recommend block-with-timeout + circuit breaker for critical routes.
[09:15] Liam: if we block, won't that exhaust GPU slots under heavy load?
[09:20] Jamal: that's why we have route prioritization and Dedicated pools; critical routes can be pinned to Dedicated nodes with isolation so blocking there doesn't starve other tenants.
[09:30] Maya: ok let's talk about benchmarking — what do you need from us to run a representative test?
[09:35] Priya: sample long-context dataset (1000 sessions), expected token distribution, target TPS, and success criteria (p99 latency, accuracy delta threshold). we'll run a 24h soak and provide raw logs + dashboard.
[09:50] Ethan: recap: we'll send pricing, benchmark runbook, SOC2 & security docs, and propose a Dedicated sizing.
[10:00] Maya: timeline — we'd like to start POC mid-april and run tests by end of april.
[10:08] Ethan: sounds good, we'll follow up with calendar invite for scoping.
[10:12] [questions wrap, some small talk]
[10:30] Liam: one last question, SDKs — we use python + go, how mature are the streaming clients?
[10:36] Priya: python and go SDKs support streaming, reconnect, idempotency keys; there are sample integrations for akka/flux if you need a reactive consumer.
[10:45] Noah: great, thanks all.
[10:48] Ethan: thanks, we'll send notes and action items. bye.

Meeting recap (auto):
- Primary ask: validate Redwood at 1k-5k TPS with mixed long-context (32k+) workloads and test streaming backpressure/timeouts.
- Decisions: run a 24h benchmark; start POC scoping; Redwood to propose Dedicated sizing.
- Risks noted: quality regression with heavy quantization, cost increase for very large context, client slow-consumer patterns.

End of transcript.
